`imr(..., marginalize = ...)` identifies the regression parameters integrated
out of the main-chain target. Integration accounts for their uncertainty; it
does not fix them at estimates. All choices use the same data preparation,
pMOM priors and availability-subgroup MRF model.

| `marginalize` | Main-chain regression state | Numerical calculation |
|---|---|---|
| `"none"` | $\beta$ and $\sigma^2$ | Joint sampling with exact local coefficient integrals |
| `"variance"` | $\beta$ | Analytic variance integral; weighted-t coefficient updates |
| `"coefficients"` | $\sigma^2$ | Polynomial-exact Gaussian integration; small models only |
| `"coefficients_and_variance"` | Neither | Retained Laplace-based selection algorithm |

The default is `"none"`. The first three methods target exact marginals of the
specified posterior, up to floating-point calculations and finite MCMC error.
The last retains the original approximation. Changing `marginalize` is an
algorithm comparison, not a performance optimization of the same algorithm.

# Common subgroup model

For one subgroup, write $z$ for its observed or augmented working response,
$X_\gamma$ for the active design, and $d$ for its number of coefficients,
including the always-active intercept and clinical terms. Let

\[
T=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_d),
\qquad
A_\gamma=a+\frac n2+\frac{3d}{2},
\]

\[
Q_\gamma(\beta)=b+\frac12
\left(\|z-X_\gamma\beta\|^2+\beta^TT^{-1}\beta\right).
\]

Multiplying the Gaussian likelihood, first-order pMOM priors and the
inverse-gamma variance prior gives the subgroup density

\[
J_\gamma(\beta,\sigma^2)
=C_\gamma\left(\prod_{j=1}^d\beta_j^2\right)
(\sigma^2)^{-A_\gamma-1}
\exp\{-Q_\gamma(\beta)/\sigma^2\},
\]

\[
C_\gamma=\frac{b^a}
{\Gamma(a)(2\pi)^{(n+d)/2}|T|^{3/2}}.
\]

The model-dependent constant matters when comparing selection states of
different dimensions. Subgroup factors multiply, with the normalized MRF prior
linking selection indicators. For binary or censored data, these are densities
of augmented responses. Observed-data evidence would also require integrating
the unobserved responses over their permitted regions.

# Sample both regression parameters

With `marginalize = "none"`, the main chain retains both parameters. A feature
update integrates its local coefficient, selects its subgroup inclusion pattern,
and immediately draws active coefficients. The variance update is

\[
\sigma^2\mid\beta,\gamma,z\sim
IG\{A_\gamma,Q_\gamma(\beta)\}.
\]

The [joint sampler guide](joint-posterior.html) derives the scalar Bayes factor,
coefficient draws, feature exchanges and latent-response updates.

# Integrate residual variance

The inverse-gamma integral gives

\[
G_\gamma(\beta)=C_\gamma\Gamma(A_\gamma)
\frac{\prod_j\beta_j^2}{Q_\gamma(\beta)^{A_\gamma}}.
\]

For a candidate coefficient, hold the other coefficients fixed and define

\[
r_j=z-\sum_{k\ne j}x_k\beta_k,
\qquad \kappa_j=x_j^Tx_j+\tau_j^{-1},
\qquad m_j=x_j^Tr_j/\kappa_j.
\]

If $d_0$ other coefficients are active, let

\[
A_0=a+n/2+3d_0/2,
\qquad
B_0=b+\frac12\left(r_j^Tr_j+\sum_{k\ne j}\beta_k^2/\tau_k\right),
\qquad B_1=B_0-\kappa_jm_j^2/2.
\]

The inclusion Bayes factor after integrating variance is

\[
\overline{B}_j=
\frac{1}{\tau_j^{3/2}\sqrt{\kappa_j}}
\left(\frac{B_0}{B_1}\right)^{A_0}
\left(\frac{A_0m_j^2}{B_1}+\frac1{\kappa_j}\right).
\]

The code evaluates $B_1$ as a sum of nonnegative residual and prior terms to
avoid subtractive cancellation. Active coefficients follow a squared-coefficient
weighted Student density:

\[
p(\beta_j\mid\gamma_j=1,\text{rest})\propto
\beta_j^2\left\{B_1+\kappa_j(\beta_j-m_j)^2/2\right\}^{-A_0-3/2}.
\]

The implementation samples this density by rejection, using a Student proposal
and its square-weighted component. Latent responses use the corresponding
truncated Student full conditionals. They do not use a variance draw from a
previous iteration. Conditional inverse-gamma recovery supplies variance draws
for summaries and prediction without affecting subsequent transitions.

# Integrate regression coefficients

Complete the square using

\[
K_\gamma=X_\gamma^TX_\gamma+T^{-1},
\qquad m_\gamma=K_\gamma^{-1}X_\gamma^Tz,
\]

\[
B_\gamma=b+\frac12
\left(z^Tz-m_\gamma^TK_\gamma m_\gamma\right),
\qquad H_\gamma=a+n/2+d.
\]

The coefficient-integrated subgroup factor is

\[
F_\gamma(\sigma^2)=D_\gamma
(\sigma^2)^{-H_\gamma-1}e^{-B_\gamma/\sigma^2}
M_\gamma(\sigma^2),
\]

\[
D_\gamma=C_\gamma(2\pi)^{d/2}|K_\gamma|^{-1/2},
\qquad
M_\gamma(\sigma^2)=
E_{U\sim N(m_\gamma,\sigma^2K_\gamma^{-1})}
\left[\prod_{j=1}^d U_j^2\right].
\]

The product moment includes coefficient correlations. The code evaluates it
with positive Gaussian quadrature after a triangular transform. Orders
$d+1,d,\ldots,2$ integrate the polynomial exactly in exact arithmetic. The
result requires $(d+1)!$ nodes. The default `max_integration_nodes = 200000`
therefore permits at most seven candidate coefficients per subgroup, including
forced terms. Fitting checks the largest candidate model before sampling and
fails if the budget is insufficient; it does not discard selection states.

The variance conditional is generally not a single inverse-gamma density.
A normal random walk on log variance uses $F_\gamma$ with the proposal ratio
$\sigma^{2\prime}/\sigma^2$. Selection and feature exchanges also use
$F_\gamma$. Latent-response proposals include the full marginal-density and
proposal-density corrections. Conditional multivariate pMOM rejection sampling
supplies coefficient draws; the primary transitions do not condition on them.

# Retain the original Laplace calculation

`marginalize = "coefficients_and_variance"` keeps the previously corrected
selection algorithm. It analytically integrates variance and uses the original
Gaussian moment approximation and Laplace calculation for coefficient
integration. Numerical tolerances, iteration caps, selection proposals and
latent-response rules remain as before. `imr_control()` exposes the existing
Laplace settings. The legacy finite survival-proposal bound is also retained;
unsupported censoring bounds raise an error.

For comparison, the exact Gaussian product moment can be written

\[
M_\gamma(\sigma^2)=\sum_{k=0}^d c_{\gamma k}(\sigma^2)^k,
\]

which would give the exact full integral

\[
m_\gamma(z)=D_\gamma\sum_{k=0}^d c_{\gamma k}
\frac{\Gamma(H_\gamma-k)}{B_\gamma^{H_\gamma-k}}.
\]

That formula is not a replacement silently applied to the original engine.
Some polynomial coefficients may be negative even though the moment is
positive, so a positive inverse-gamma-mixture interpretation does not follow.

The retained engine uses its Gamma interaction proposals. The other three use
log-normal proposals; both include the normalized MRF target and their proposal
corrections. Runtime differences consequently reflect more than which
regression parameters are marginalized.

# Summaries and comparison

The first three choices store full regression draws. They perform auxiliary
recovery on every sweep so that thinning or retaining latent output does not
change the primary random stream. Log-density traces describe each algorithm's
own target and are not comparable model-evidence scores.

A Laplace fit stores selection and interaction draws. Its `predict()` method
keeps the original rescored-state point approximation. Optional
`sample_regression_posterior()` returns conditional regression draws with the
empirical selection weights. Conditional-chain diagnostics cannot replace the
source selection-chain diagnostics; short chains do not guarantee exact
conditional reconstruction.

Use the same data, priors and preprocessing when comparing algorithms, and
report their budgets, starts, effective sample sizes, uncertainty and elapsed
time. Matching posterior conclusions is a Monte Carlo question for the first
three choices. Comparisons with the retained original algorithm must also allow
for Laplace approximation error. Optimization of one fixed algorithm has a
stricter regression criterion: preserve its arithmetic precision, full output
and random stream under the same build and settings.
